nodes.title: Interpretations on definable quotients
nodes.statement: For languages L_A,L_B and nonempty native structures A,B, an interpretation I of B in A consists of a finite arity m, an A-parameter-definable D⊆A^m, a definable equivalence E on D, a bijection D/E≃B, and definable E-invariant pullbacks of every relation and function graph of L_B. Function graphs must be total on D and single valued modulo E. A finite tuple of parameters is part of the data. There is no definable choice of representatives requirement.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.locator: §1, Theorems 1.1–1.2, pp.1–4; §5, Facts 5.2 and final proof, pp.16–18 (arXiv v2)
sources.match: Arithmetic fields are accessed through definable domains and quotients, with parameters and composite interpretation maps tracked.

proofSteps: Use the existing definable-set predicate for D, the kernel and symbol graphs. Form the native setoid quotient and transport the B-structure along the supplied bijection.
Translate terms by their graph formulas. Translate equality by E; relativize existential quantifiers to D and use kernel invariance for independence of representatives.
acceptance: D=A, E=equality and identity symbol graphs recover the original native structure.
For an integral domain R, pairs (a,b) with b≠0 and relation ad=bc interpret Frac(R); (1,2) and (2,4) have the same class when 2≠0.
The graph assigning both 0 and 1 to one input over a two-element equality quotient fails the function uniqueness axiom.
A definable ideal I gives R/I by a quotient; no definable transversal is required.

nodes.title: Semantics and composition of interpretations
nodes.statement: An interpretation I:B in A gives, for every finite tuple of B-elements and any representatives in D, equivalence between realization of a B-formula and realization of its translated A-formula. Composing interpretations C in B and B in A gives C in A; its parameter tuple includes representatives of the inner parameters and its domain, kernel and symbol formulas are obtained by translation. Identity interpretations act as identities up to definable quotient isomorphism.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

proofSteps: Induct over native formulas: equality uses E; symbol atoms use their defining graphs; Boolean operations are native; quantified witnesses range over D and quotient surjectivity supplies representatives.
For composition flatten the two finite tuples, translate the inner domain and equivalence, and apply the first semantic equivalence twice. No elimination of imaginaries is assumed.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Parametric bi-interpretations
nodes.statement: A parametric bi-interpretation between A and B consists of interpretations in both directions and definable isomorphisms of each composite interpretation with the identity on its ambient structure, over the accumulated finite parameter tuples. nodes.title: A chosen nonstandard arithmetic extension
nodes.statement: Fix a nonprincipal ultrafilter U on ℕ and form the already native ultrapower *ℕ=(U:Filter ℕ).Product(λ_,ℕ) in the arithmetic language. nodes.title: Standard parts with explicit domains
nodes.statement: On finite native hyperreals, the native standard part is the unique real infinitesimally close to the input, preserves addition and multiplication on that finite subring, and fixes embedded reals. The native total function has default values outside this domain: stdPart(omega)=0 does not make omega infinitesimally close to zero. For the chosen arithmetic ultrapower use standard remainders modulo each fixed positive integer instead. No global ring retraction *ℕ→ℕ is asserted; any comparison to native hyperreals requires a same-ultrafilter adapter.

nodes.title: The Denef–Pas language
nodes.statement: Use a tagged disjoint union of the valued-field, residue-field and value-group carriers to encode a three-sorted language in native first-order syntax. The first two sorts have ring language; the third has Presburger +,−,0,1,≤ and congruences modulo every positive integer. Cross-sort symbols are ord:VF×→VG and ac:VF→RF; a total ord on VF is allowed only with a specified value at 0 and every genuine valuation comparison guarded against 0. Quantifiers are relativized to their named sort. Coefficients and extra constants are recorded by a parameter diagram.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

nodes.title: Angular components and valued structures
nodes.statement: A Denef–Pas valued structure consists of a nontrivially valued henselian field K, its native valuation subring O, residue field k, a chosen surjective additive normalization ord:K×→Γ with Γ≡ℤ in Presburger language, and a map ac:K→k satisfying ac(0)=0, ac(xy)=ac(x)ac(y), and ac(u)=res(u) for units u∈O. nodes.statement: For a fixed sentence in the coefficient-free Denef–Pas language, its truth in sufficiently large residue-characteristic local fields is determined by the isomorphism class of the residue field, provided the two fields carry the stipulated ac and Presburger structures. There exists a bound N depending on that sentence; this gives the same truth for ℚ_p and ℤ/pℤ((t)) for all sufficiently large primes p. The assertion is eventual, with no claimed effective or uniform-in-all-formulas N.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

nodes.title: Residue dimension detects divisorial valuations
nodes.statement: Let K be finitely generated over its prime field and v any valuation. If dim_Kr(Kv)=dim_Kr(K)−1, then its valuation ring is a DVR and Kv is finitely generated over its prime field; hence v is a prime divisor. Discreteness, finite rank and residue finite generation are conclusions. Finite generation of K is essential.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.locator: §1, p.2, Engler–Prestel Theorem 3.4.3 citation; direct finite-basis proof specified here
sources.match: The criterion itself is cited in the paper; the plan supplies an elementary Gauss-subfield route rather than claiming a full reading of the cited book.

proofSteps: The equality excludes the trivial valuation. In equal characteristic lift a residue transcendence basis to units; the prime field is trivially valued. Adjoin an element of positive value. Distinct powers have different values, so this element is transcendental over the lifted residue subfield. Dimension equality makes K finite over that one-variable rational subfield.

In mixed characteristic with residue characteristic p, lift a residue transcendence basis. The restriction to ℚ is a multiple of v_p; reduction of polynomials with unit coefficients identifies the Gauss value group as ℤ·v(p) and its residue as a rational field over 𝔽_p. K is finite over this Gauss subfield.

For a finite valued-field extension, choose elements of distinct value cosets and independent residue lifts; their products are linearly independent. Thus e·f≤[K:K₀], giving finite value-group index and finite residue degree.

An ordered abelian group with a finite-index cyclic subgroup is cyclic: embed it in (1/e)ℤ by multiplying by the finite index. Convert a least positive generator into the native DVR criterion. The finite residue extension of a rational field is finitely generated.
acceptance: No hypothesis assumes the value group is already cyclic.
The infinite purely inseparable tower 𝔽_p(t^(1/p^∞)) shows why finite generation cannot be dropped.

nodes.title: Kronecker dimension drops under valuation
nodes.statement: For any field K of finite absolute transcendence degree and any nontrivial valuation v, dim_Kr(Kv)<dim_Kr K. In characteristic (0,0), a henselian coefficient-field route is allowed only after its existence theorem is supplied; the direct residue-lift proof avoids that extra input.

nodes.title: Coarsening from an infinitely large coefficient

Put Δ={γ∈Γ: N|γ|<d for every N>0} and p={0}∪{x∈O_w∖{0}: d≤Nw(x) for some N>0}. Then Δ is convex, p is prime, a_d∈p and every nonzero lower coefficient a_i is outside p. For nonnegative values, membership outside Δ is the displayed existential cut. Valuation inequalities prove ideal closure, and if neither value crosses the cut then neither does their sum, proving primality.

The quotient valuation ring equals localization at p: values in Δ become units, and the ordered quotient has nonnegative image exactly when a denominator outside p clears the original value. Reuse current coarsenByUnits rather than reconstructing it.

nodes.title: Measures attached to gauge forms

nodes.title: Definable subassignments
nodes.statement: Fix a characteristic-zero base field k and named coefficients in k((t)). A map is specified by one uniformly definable graph that is a function in every K. This is a subassignment of point sets; it need not be a subfunctor under arbitrary field extensions because quantified formulas need not be extension invariant. Gluing along finite algebraic charts is a separate global construction.

nodes.title: Universal definition of integers in rationals
nodes.statement: There is a parameter-free universal first-order formula in the ring language defining ℤ⊂ℚ; equivalently ℚ∖ℤ is Diophantine over ℚ. For a nonempty finite S and R=∩_{ℓ∈S}ℤ_(ℓ), the source universal predicate R̃={x:¬∃y∈Jac(R),xy=1} equals ⋃_{ℓ∈S}ℤ_(ℓ), not R itself. All guards have existential descriptions, so their implications can be placed under universal quantifiers. Negate the resulting formula and combine equations using formal reality of ℚ.

nodes.title: Rational-model preservation criteria
nodes.statement: For K⊂L both models of Th(ℚ), let Z_K,Z_L be defined by a fixed universal integer formula. Then (a) Z_L∩K⊂Z_K; (b) Z_L∩K is integrally closed in K; (c) for every positive n, L^n∩K=K^n, so K is radically closed in L. Conditionally, if ℤ is Diophantine in ℚ, then (d) Z_L∩K=Z_K and K is relatively algebraically closed in L. More generally, ℤ has an existential definition in ℚ iff Z_K⊂Z_L for every such embedding. Finally Th(ℚ) is not model complete: model completeness would make every definable rational subset existential, contradicting the non-RE complement of an RE undecidable subset of the defined integer ring. No unconditional existential integer definition follows.

sources.match: Universal preservation, radical closure and the existential-definability criterion are distinct conclusions.

In that invariant case a=q_K^(−dn)N. Define P_K,t(T)=Σ_n a_K,t,n T^n. A local density is a specified limit of a chosen normalization only when existence has been proved; it is not the raw count N.

nodes.title: Singular-fibre integral for the product map
nodes.statement: For a nonarchimedean local field with residue size q and Haar mass µ(O)=1, the number of residue-field solutions of xy=0 is 2q−1. Over nonzero a∈m, the fibre of xy=a in O² is parametrized by |a|≤|x|≤1 with relative density |dx/x|, whose mass is (v(a)+1)(1−q^−1). Integrating this mass over a∈m∖{0} and multiplying by q² gives 2q−1. The singular fibre a=0 is not a smooth fibre endowed with that relative formula.

nodes.title: Definable dimension, choice and finite topology
nodes.statement: For a fixed o-minimal expansion, dimension is the maximum dimension of a cell in an adapted finite decomposition, independent of decomposition, with dim∅=−∞. Each definable set has finitely many connected components, each definable and definably path connected, uniformly bounded in a definable family. Every definable surjection admits a definable section. A definable set with finitely many distinguished definable subsets admits a definable triangulation onto a union of open simplices of a finite complex, compatible with those subsets; it need not be a closed polyhedron.

nodes.title: Definable analytic boundary comparison
nodes.statement: Import DifferentialGeometry’s abstract boundary ∂̃X of pairs (x,local boundary face at x), of dimension n−1 for n>0, and its immersion i_X:∂̃X→X. Give it the analytic and finite-definable chart certificates induced by a finite analytic/definable corner atlas. At a point of depth k the fibre of i_X has k elements; it need not be injective. nodes.title: Restricted-analytic structure of compact corners
nodes.statement: Every compact real analytic n-manifold with corners has a canonical R_an-definable structure compatible with its analytic atlas. Its abstract boundary immersion and interior inclusion are definable. Canonical means independent of the chosen finite refinement by relatively compact semianalytic charts whose transitions extend analytically over compact neighbourhoods; it does not mean that every analytic chart is globally restricted analytic.

nodes.title: Definably proper equivalence-relation quotients
nodes.statement: Let X⊂ℝ^n be locally closed and definable in the fixed o-minimal structure. Let E⊂X×X be a closed definable equivalence relation whose coordinate projections to X are definably proper. The intended quotient contract is a Hausdorff definable space Q and continuous definable quotient map q:X→Q, with q(x)=q(y) iff E(x,y), the quotient topology and factorization of continuous definable E-invariant maps. In particular, for a semialgebraic group G and compact semialgebraic subgroup M, G/M has its semialgebraic quotient and semialgebraic G-action. The exact general quotient theorem is a source gap; the compact-group application is the checked input.

nodes.title: Definable exponential cover on bounded sectors
nodes.statement: For fixed R>0 and c∈ℝ, the map z↦exp(2πiz) on 0<Re(z)<R, Im(z)>c is R_an,exp-definable, as are its finite products and restrictions to ordered-imaginary-part sectors. The sine and cosine factors have bounded real arguments, so they are restricted analytic after rescaling; exp(−2πIm(z)) uses the real exponential. If a holomorphic Ψ extends across a neighbourhood of a closed smaller polydisk, then Ψ composed with this cover is definable on a sector whose image lies in that smaller disk.

nodes.title: Wider-sector rational curve test
nodes.statement: Use coefficient germs and localization expressions defined on every finite-width ordered sector, with their nonvanishing/rough bounds checked separately for each width. Let f be a rough polynomial localization element and g a signed rough monomial there. Assume that for every finite width R and every rational-slope affine diagonal curve with fixed trailing coordinates, |f|≤C_curve|g| on its intersection with Σ_n^R. Then for each fixed R there is C_R with |f|≤C_R|g| on Σ_n^R. The curve constants need not be uniform across curves. This strengthened-width version is the planned repair of BKT Lemma 4.5; a hypothesis confined to width one is not substituted.

This does not control an unbounded earlier variable y_j with j<i or turn the complement of y_n≫1 into a compact set.

nodes.title: Definable structure of complex algebraic varieties
nodes.statement: A complex algebraic variety of finite type acquires its canonical R_alg-definable space structure by finite affine charts, identifying ℂ^n with ℝ^(2n). For smooth varieties this is a definable complex manifold; singular varieties retain a finite definable space atlas without a false manifold assertion. Morphisms are definable, and finite affine-cover refinements give the same structure.

nodes.title: Definable complex analytic Chow theorem
nodes.statement: If Y is a complex quasiprojective variety and A⊂Y is closed in Y, complex analytic and definable in the fixed o-minimal expansion (with the hypotheses of the chosen analytic-closure theorem), then A is algebraic. For a smooth Y and an expansion containing R_an this includes BKT Theorem 4.13. Boolean combinations of closed definable complex analytic sets are constructible algebraic. Closedness is relative to Y, not necessarily to a projective compactification.

nodes.title: Definability of continuous dense extensions
nodes.statement: Let U be a dense definable subset of a definable topological space X, and f:U→Y a definable map to a Hausdorff definable space. If a continuous extension f̄:X→Y exists, then it is unique and definable: its graph equals the closure of graph(f) in X×Y. This is an extension certificate, not an existence theorem. In finite charts the graph-closure calculation uses the actual relative topologies.

nodes.title: Uniform bounded-derivative parametrization
nodes.statement: For every finite r≥1 and definable family X⊂(0,1)^n×ℝ^m, there is N such that every nonempty fibre X_t is covered by at most N definable C^r maps from (0,1)^dim(X_t) into X_t, with every derivative of order ≤r bounded in absolute value by 1. Empty fibres use no charts. Maps on nonempty fibres may be repeated to use a common finite bound, and the zero-dimensional case is a finite set of constant maps from a singleton. This is a finite-order theorem; no uniform bound for all r is claimed.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.locator: Theorems 2.3 and 2.5, pp.597–599; proof §§3–5, pp.599–609; Corollaries 5.1–5.2, p.609

proofSteps: Prove the one-variable derivative normalization by monotonicity and inverse changes of variable.

Rescale finitely many domain cubes to turn a fixed derivative bound into 1; obtain family uniformity by definable choice and saturation.

In Corollary 4.4 replace the incorrect higher chain rule identity on p.607 by the full finite Faà di Bruno expansion. Induct on the last-coordinate derivative order: every product uses previously controlled composed derivatives and bounded derivatives of the one-variable reparametrization. This proves boundedness without the false single-product identity (E23).

nodes.statement: For k<n and each degree d≥1 there are r(k,n,d), C>0 and η(k,n,d)>0 with η→0 as d→∞ such that the rational points of height ≤T in the image of a C^r map (0,1)^k→ℝ^n whose derivatives up to r are bounded by 1 lie on at most C T^η real algebraic hypersurfaces of degree ≤d, for every T≥1. nodes.title: Definable semialgebraic blocks
nodes.statement: A basic block of dimension d is a connected definable C¹-regular subset U of a semialgebraic C¹ locus A of the same dimension d, locally open in that locus; include a singleton at d=0. A block is a continuous semialgebraic image of a basic block, with the map defined on a semialgebraic set containing it. Families carry these conditions fibrewise. Blocks may be definable without being semialgebraic as entire sets. Positive-dimensional blocks contained in X lie in X_alg.

For positive dimension, cover a definable path by finitely many semialgebraic neighbourhoods and replace its pieces by semialgebraic paths.

nodes.title: Uniform rational and integral block counting
nodes.statement: For every definable family X and ε>0 there are finitely many basic block families contained fibrewise in X and C>0 such that all rational points of height ≤T in each fibre are covered by at most C T^ε of their blocks, uniformly for T≥1 and the family parameter. The same applies to integral points with maximum absolute coordinate ≤T. Under a continuous semialgebraic map from the family, the images are at most that many blocks; positive-dimensional image blocks lie in the algebraic part of the image, whereas zero-dimensional blocks are single points.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: The refinement keeps the regular full-dimensional pieces arising in the original counting induction.

proofSteps: Retain the finitely many families of regular semialgebraic pieces in the PW dimension induction rather than only their union.
Cover the rational points by the resulting O(T^ε) individual fibres.
Use the block image definition and integral-to-rational height equality for the two consumer forms.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Counting algebraic points of bounded degree
nodes.statement: Fix k≥1, a definable family X and ε>0. The points x in each fibre whose real coordinates are algebraic of degree individually ≤k and absolute multiplicative Weil height ≤T are covered by at most C(X,k,ε)T^ε blocks. Consequently the number outside X_alg has that bound. Encode each coordinate by a nonzero coefficient vector (a₀,…,a_k) of length k+1 and polynomial Σ_{j=0}^k a_j t^j; the k-coefficient author-copy indexing is corrected explicitly.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.6, p.2; §5, Lemma 5.2 and Theorem 5.3, pp.7–8; ao §6.2–6.3, pp.387–388
sources.match: Finite semialgebraic root branches transfer block covers from coefficient space to algebraic coordinates.

proofSteps: Use DT.0 to find a coefficient vector of height ≤2^kT^k for every coordinate.
Partition the nonzero coefficient space into semialgebraic strata with continuous ordered real-root branches; a polynomial of degree ≤k has at most k roots.
Apply block counting in coefficient space with exponent smaller than ε/k and push blocks through these root branches.
Use Northcott only after fixing the coordinatewise degree and height bounds.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Semi-rational counting and marked projections
nodes.statement: For a definable family F_t⊂ℝ^m×ℝ^n, fixed algebraic degree bound k and ε>0, there is C such that if Σ consists of points (y,z)∈F_t with degree/height bound k,T on y alone and #π₂Σ>C T^ε, there is a continuous definable β:[0,1]→F_t with π₁β semialgebraic and analytic on (0,1), π₂β nonconstant, and π₂β(0)∈π₂Σ. If the structure has analytic cell decomposition, β can be made analytic on (0,1). The conclusion does not state β(0)∈Σ after that analytic rescaling.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: The marked object preserved by rescaling is the second projection, not the complete starting point.

proofSteps: Separate isolated and nonisolated fibres over y. A nonisolated point supplies a definable path with y fixed.
For isolated fibres use uniform finite fibre bounds and definable choice to split into finitely many graphs of continuous definable functions.
Cover their algebraic y-coordinates by O(T^ε) blocks and use pigeonhole to choose two different z-values in one graph.
Join them by a semialgebraic path in the base block. Rescale the first interval with nonconstant second projection; this preserves π₂β(0) but need not preserve y(0).

For Theorem 7.1 isolate the zero-dimensional fibres by a quantified local-isolation formula. In adapted cells use dim C_y=dim C−dim π(C), not dim C−1 for an m-dimensional parameter block; the latter printed claim is E24.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Orbit growth versus definable counting
nodes.statement: Let X be a fixed definable family of lifts of special points, and suppose independent arithmetic inputs give, for each special point s of complexity D_s, at least cD_s^δ distinct lifts in its fibre, each with coordinatewise degree ≤k and height ≤CD_s^A, for fixed c,C,δ,A>0 and k. For ε with Aε<δ and D_s sufficiently large, at least one such lift lies in a positive-dimensional block of X_s. To deduce a special subvariety through s, the separate functional-transcendence theorem must apply to the corresponding block and the chosen lift.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: Arithmetic orbit lower bounds, polynomial lift heights and algebraic-degree counting are three separate inputs.

proofSteps: Insert T=CD_s^A into the uniform block estimate and compare exponents.
For large D_s the number of lifts exceeds the number of singleton blocks, so some lift lies in a positive-dimensional block.
Use only the separately supplied semialgebraic-to-complex-algebraic and Ax–Lindemann implication to identify a geometric locus.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Finite exceptional CM points
nodes.statement: For an algebraic V⊂A_g defined over a number field, only finitely many CM points in V avoid all positive-dimensional special subvarieties contained in V. Assume the A_g uniformization definability, independent polynomial Galois-orbit lower bound, polynomial lift-height bound with degree ≤2g per coordinate, and the source Ax–Lindemann theorem. Bounded remaining complexity gives finiteness by the supplied height bound and bounded-degree Northcott.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: The point-level counting argument precedes the induction on positive-dimensional special loci.
The conjugate-point counting step and Galois transport precede the family induction.
The hyperbolic Ax–Lindemann comparison is imported from LogicAndDefinabilityPartII; this source supplies the precise complex statement, not a proof.

proofSteps: Replace the irreducible component under consideration by the closure of its CM points, which descends to a number field.
Apply the orbit-counting bridge only to lifts of CM points outside the positive-dimensional special locus.
For unbounded complexity the bridge contradicts that exclusion. For bounded complexity apply the independent height bound and Northcott.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Finite special families and dimension induction
nodes.statement: In the source A_g setting, import the finite-family theorem for maximal special subvarieties: finitely many algebraic normal-factor parameter loci and finite maps V₀×S→V cover the maximal positive-dimensional special subvarieties as fibres over isolated special parameters, with V₀ containing no positive-dimensional special subvariety. Combine finite exceptional special points on those parameter loci with induction on dimension to obtain finitely many maximal special subvarieties. Definability of a countable union alone does not imply an arbitrary family is finite; the algebraic-family and maximality hypotheses are retained.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.locator: §6.5, p.388, citing Pila–Tsimerman §7; routed normalizer/family refinements
sources.match: The final family reduction is a separate geometric supplier, not an automatic consequence of point counting.
Both normalizer branches and the finite-family reduction were read; their geometric objects are imported from the shared Part II.

proofSteps: Use reductivity of the relevant connected normalizers to obtain finitely many special envelopes for each subgroup type.
Use definability of the weakly-special union and the normal-factor algebraic parameter locus to reduce to finitely many families.
Maximal fibres correspond to isolated special parameters; apply the point result to those parameter loci.
Transport special subvarieties from a Galois conjugate back to the original variety, and induct on the strictly smaller parameter dimensions.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: André–Oort theorem for A_g
nodes.statement: For every g≥1 and every algebraic subvariety V of the complex moduli space A_g of principally polarized g-dimensional abelian varieties, the Zariski closure of its CM points is a finite union of special subvarieties. The statement is unconditional in the cited source: its orbit bound uses averaged Colmez and isogeny estimates as independent geometric/arithmetic inputs. Counting and family induction establish this exact A_g case; no arbitrary mixed-Shimura André–Oort theorem is asserted.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: This is the source-scoped application endpoint.

proofSteps: Pass to irreducible components of the CM closure and descend each to a number field.
Use finite exceptional CM points and the finite-special-family induction to show that a positive-dimensional component is special.
Include zero-dimensional components as special points.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: CM-pair finiteness on a nonmodular curve
nodes.statement: For an irreducible algebraic curve C⊂ℂ² that is neither a horizontal/vertical special line nor a modular correspondence Φ_m=0, only finitely many points of C have both coordinates CM j-invariants. Use the A_1×A_1 André–Oort supplier or its precise modular-curve reduction, rather than applying the A_g statement to an unspecified embedding. In the Masser–Zannier application the curve f(y₁,y₂)=0 is absolutely irreducible and involves both variables; its nonmodularity excludes the positive-dimensional special alternatives.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: The application needs the exact special-curve classification and absolute irreducibility.

proofSteps: Import the modular special-curve classification and the André–Oort case for the product of modular curves.
Intersect C with the finite union of special components in its CM closure; an infinite set would force C itself to be one of the excluded special curves.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Hermitian arithmetic and algebraic structure comparison
nodes.statement: For a Hermitian symmetric arithmetic quotient with the compact subgroup fixed as a maximal compact K, compare its finite-atlas Borel–Serre R_an structure with the R_alg structure of its complex algebraic model only after passing to R_an,exp. The identity is R_an,exp-definable in both directions; the two structures need not agree in R_an. Import the precise geometric uniformization/comparison theorem from its owner. Quotient functoriality uses the fixed K and Cartan-involution-compatible morphisms of the 2023 BKT erratum. No second arithmetic quotient or algebraic compactification is constructed here.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.1(1)–(2), Example 1.2 and subsequent Hermitian comparison discussion, pp.3–4; Theorems 4.12–4.13, p.18; separate 2023 erratum
sources.match: BKT explicitly distinguishes the Borel–Serre and algebraic R_an structures and describes the R_an,exp comparison. There is no Theorem 1.1(4); the exact geometric comparison remains an imported contract.
The compact subgroup is fixed and morphisms require the corrected Cartan compatibility.

proofSteps: Import the fixed-K quotient and algebraic-model comparison with its precise geometric hypotheses. BKT Example 1.2 and its following discussion distinguish the two R_an structures; the general definable comparison is a supplier contract, not a conclusion of Theorem 1.1 alone.

On a finite cover express the comparison using the supplied uniformizing maps in R_an,exp and glue their definable graphs. Closure under inverse graphs gives the reverse definable identity. Definable Chow applies to a closed complex-analytic graph only after definability and its ambient hypotheses are established; it cannot manufacture this comparison.
acceptance: The comparison is stated in R_an,exp, with K fixed and the corrected morphism restrictions.

For the modular cusp a Borel–Serre inverse-height coordinate t gives the algebraic cusp coordinate exp(−2π/t). Extending by zero at t=0 gives a nonanalytic flat germ, so the comparison need not be R_an-definable.
Definable Chow is used only after the comparison graph is known definable, complex analytic and closed in its specified algebraic ambient space.

nodes.title: Abelian Ax-type image interface
nodes.statement: For a fixed complex abelian variety A of dimension g and a real analytic group isomorphism A(C)≃(ℝ/ℤ)^(2g), import abelian Ax: the image X of a closed algebraic subvariety is Ax-type. Thus every continuous semialgebraic path in a lift of X, analytic on its interior, has exponential image in a coset through its starting point of a closed subtorus, that coset contained in X. For the group-action conclusion additionally assume Z is an irreducible closed algebraic subvariety of A, Γ preserves Z, Γ acts faithfully on A, contains a free subgroup on two generators, fixes no nonzero vector of ℤ^(2g), and is of monodromy type: every abelian subvariety B⊂A is preserved by every γ∈Γ. Then Z lies in a proper torsion coset or has a positive-dimensional abelian stabilizer. The separate marked-endpoint counting gap must be repaired before this application proof is closed.
hypotheses: The Ax-type assertion concerns closed algebraic subvarieties. The additional group-action conclusion requires irreducibility, Γ-invariance and every monodromy-type/group-action hypothesis displayed in the statement.

sources.match: The real definability and counting inputs are separate from abelian Ax and the group-action assumptions.

proofSteps: Restrict the exponential/lattice uniformization to a compact fundamental box to obtain R_an definability.

Choose c≥2 bounding the Euclidean operator norms of both generators and both inverses. Submultiplicativity gives H(γ)≤c^length(γ); free-word growth then supplies many rational matrix/translation coordinates. This repairs the repeated-generator constant in E25.
Apply only the corrected semi-rational marked-parameter result, then the imported Ax theorem.
Use countability of subtori and Baire category for a common stabilizer on a nonempty open set; use monodromy invariance and algebraicity for the abelian conclusion.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Complex period codimension consequence
nodes.statement: In Lawrence–Sawin’s polarized integral Hodge–Deligne system on a smooth irreducible complex base X of positive dimension, let Φ_C from its universal cover take values in the monodromy flag variety G_mon/P. If an algebraic Z⊂(G_mon/P)_ℂ has codimension at least dim X, then every irreducible component of Φ_C⁻¹(Z) projects into a proper algebraic subvariety of X. Import the precise Bakker–Tsimerman Ax–Schanuel theorem for the associated polarized pure variation and its monodromy domain. The p-adic comparison and formal-to-rigid transport in the subsequent theorem are outside this complex logical interface.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: Apply Ax–Schanuel to X×Z and the period graph, retaining the independent Hodge and monodromy inputs.

proofSteps: Treat a zero-dimensional inverse-image component separately.
For a positive-dimensional component U in the period graph W, compute codim(W)=dim(G_mon/P) and codim(X×Z)≥dim X.
The positive dimension gives the strict Ax–Schanuel codimension inequality. Import its proper weak-Mumford–Tate conclusion and project to the proper algebraic locus of X.
acceptance: The conclusion uses exactly the displayed hypotheses and the indicated prerequisite interfaces.

nodes.title: Integer polynomials as native polynomial functions
nodes.statement: For every type α, construct the ring homomorphism Tα from MvPolynomial α ℤ to Poly α which sends each integer constant c to Poly.const(c) and each variable Xᵢ to Poly.proj(i). Its underlying function evaluates the polynomial on natural assignments after casting them to integers.
hypotheses: α and β are arbitrary types, possibly empty or infinite. Natural-number assignments are cast coordinatewise to integers. Additional hypotheses are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Use the existing commutative ring on Poly α; the integer cast there is its constant constructor. Apply MvPolynomial.eval₂Hom to Int.castRingHom and Poly.proj. This supplies the ring-map laws without a second ring structure.

The constant and variable API laws follow directly from eval₂Hom_C and eval₂Hom_X'. Evaluate pointwise using Poly.ext, const_apply and proj_apply; the key evaluation theorem identifies the map with the intended polynomial function. No second polynomial carrier is introduced.
acceptance: With no variables, the image of constant −3 evaluates to −3 on the unique assignment.
At (1,3), the image of X₀−2X₁ has value −5, not a truncated natural difference.
Evaluation agrees with native MvPolynomial.eval at every natural assignment cast to integers.
The images of X₀ and X₁ in two variables differ: assignment (0,1) distinguishes them.

nodes.title: Polynomial ring equivalence
nodes.statement: For every α, bundle Tα as a ring equivalence Eα: MvPolynomial α ℤ ≃ Poly α. Its inverse sends a native polynomial function to the unique multivariate integer polynomial with the same values on every natural assignment. The inverse is classical and carries no computability assertion.

proofSteps: Combine the separately proved injectivity and surjectivity into bijectivity.
Apply RingEquiv.ofBijective. Record that the resulting forward ring map is exactly Tα. Its inverse laws and algebraic compatibility are inherited from the ring equivalence.
Evaluate Eα(Eα⁻¹(f))=f and apply to-dioph-poly-eval to obtain the inverse evaluation law. Uniqueness follows from injectivity, not from a chosen syntactic representative.

nodes.title: Preservation of existential natural roots
nodes.statement: Let h:Fin m→β be injective, q∈ℤ[α⊕Fin m], and x:α→ℕ. There exists y:β→ℕ with rename(idα⊕h,q)(x,y)=0 if and only if there exists z:Fin m→ℕ with q(x,z)=0. All evaluations cast naturals into integers.
hypotheses: α and β are arbitrary types, possibly empty or infinite. Natural-number assignments are cast coordinatewise to integers. Additional hypotheses are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Given y, restrict it to z=y∘h. MvPolynomial.eval_rename proves the evaluations agree.
Given z, use Function.extend(h,z,0) as a β-assignment. Function.Injective.extend_apply gives y(h(j))=z(j), so the same evaluation identity gives a root of the renamed polynomial.
The default zero supplies all unused witnesses, including when m=0. No surjectivity of h is needed.
acceptance: For q(u,v)=u−v−1, collapsing both witnesses makes the equation unsatisfiable although q has natural roots; the injectivity hypothesis cannot be dropped.

nodes.title: Finite Diophantine normal form
nodes.statement: For every type α and S⊆(α→ℕ), native Dioph(S) holds exactly when there are m∈ℕ and p∈MvPolynomial (α⊕Fin m) ℤ such that, for every input x, x∈S if and only if there exists y:Fin m→ℕ with eval(cast∘Sum.elim(x,y),p)=0. This holds without assuming α finite.
hypotheses: α and β are arbitrary types, possibly empty or infinite. Natural-number assignments are cast coordinatewise to integers. Additional hypotheses are stated explicitly.
proofSteps: Unpack native Dioph(S) as a polynomial function f on α⊕β and its existential-root characterization. Apply the inverse of poly-mvpolynomial-equiv to obtain integer polynomial syntax with exactly the same values.
Apply finite-right-rename to that polynomial. Then right-rename-solutions replaces the arbitrary β-witness block by Fin m while fixing x; this proves the forward implication.

For the reverse implication in universe zero use witness type Fin m and native polynomial T(p). Apply to-dioph-poly-eval. For an arbitrary input universe use the witness type ULift(Fin m) at that universe and rename p along idα⊕ULift.up before applying T. Lifting or lowering assignments gives the same existential condition by MvPolynomial.eval_rename.
This is a mathematical existential normal form, not a computable procedure for recovering p or m from a proof of native Dioph. Computable encodings and the MRDP simulation remain separate work.
acceptance: Even natural inputs are represented by X−2Y.
A nonzero constant polynomial has no root, including with zero inputs and witnesses.
The statement specializes both to finite tuples and to α=ℕ.
Zero witness variables means a polynomial condition, not automatic truth.

nodes.title: Two-universal-variable integer formula
nodes.statement: For t∈ℚ, let u=(u₁,u₂,u₃,u₄), v=(v₂,v₃,v₄), A(u)=Σᵢuᵢ², B=a u₂²+b u₃²−ab u₄², and C=a v₂²+b v₃²−ab v₄². Put F=(a+A(u))(b+A(u))((u₁²−B−1)²+((t−2u₁)²−4C−4)²). Then t∈ℤ iff for every a,b∈ℚ there exist u∈ℚ⁴,v∈ℚ³ with F=0. This displayed polynomial has degree at most 8 in the seven existential coordinates and total degree 12 when a,b,t are also variables; no total-degree-8 claim is made.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: The two-universal/seven-existential normal form is kept separately from the subsequent universal formula, with its degree convention explicit.

proofSteps: For a,b>0 the two guard factors are nonzero, so F=0 gives two norm-one quaternion traces whose sum is t. Apply the semilocal trace description and intersect over the positive parameters to recover ℤ.
If a≤0 or b≤0, four rational squares represent its negative after clearing a square denominator; choose the shared u tuple to make the corresponding guard factor zero.
For positive a,b and integral t the trace-sum theorem supplies u and v. The highest existential degree is 8; the monomial a²b²u₄⁸ has coefficient 1, certifying total degree 12.
acceptance: There are exactly two universally quantified and seven existentially quantified rational variables.
Degenerate nonpositive parameters are discharged by a guard factor, never by assuming they are positive.
The degree convention distinguishes existential-block degree from total degree.

nodes.title: Finite reduction of a definable algebraic union
nodes.statement: Let A be a complex quasiprojective variety and (Vᵢ) a countable family of closed complex algebraic subvarieties. If X=⋃ᵢVᵢ is definable in R_an,exp, then X is a finite subunion. The proof uses finite real analytic cell decomposition for this selected structure; arbitrary o-minimal expansions are not silently assigned analytic cells. Closedness and algebraicity of the Vᵢ are retained.
hypotheses: All parameters, coefficient structures and characteristic restrictions are part of the statement; definability never silently removes parameters.

sources.match: Finite analytic cells plus Baire and polynomial identity continuation give the finite subunion.

proofSteps: Take a finite decomposition of X into connected real analytic cells in R_an,exp. Its original analytic-cell theorem is included in the selected-structure source gap.
On one such cell U, the relatively closed analytic sets U∩Vᵢ form a countable cover. Baire category gives one intersection with nonempty interior.
Each polynomial vanishing on Vᵢ then vanishes on a nonempty open part of U and hence all of connected analytic U. Thus U lies in Vᵢ. Select one index for each of finitely many cells.
acceptance: A countable union of points filling the rational numbers is not definable in an o-minimal real structure.
The theorem does not assert that a general countable definable family has a finite subcover.
Every polynomial identity is continued within one connected real analytic cell.

sourceIssues.printed: The printed class of Laurent polynomials multiplied by arbitrary roughly monomial rational functions is not closed under addition.
sourceIssues.correction: Use the image of S⁻¹A in actual functions, where A=O[x_i,y_i^±1] and S consists of the elements of A whose absolute values are roughly monomial on the specified sector. This is a stricter repaired ring, not an asserted equality with the printed class; its curve theorem and Hodge-consumer compatibility remain gaps.
sourceIssues.reason: Put c=(x−1/2)²+y⁻² and k=(c+y⁻¹)/(c+2y⁻¹) on 0<x<1,y>1. The rational function k and its inverse are bounded above and below. Thus 1/k and −1 satisfy the printed roughly-polynomial condition. Their sum u=y⁻¹/(c+y⁻¹) is not roughly polynomial: if u=P/h with h comparable to y^r and P a finite Laurent polynomial in x,y with the specified analytic q=e^(2πiz) coefficients, then for each fixed x≠1/2, P has size comparable to y^(r−1), while at x=1/2 it has size comparable to y^r. The q=0 leading coefficients of P are polynomials in x. Every coefficient of degree at least r must vanish on the open set x≠1/2 and hence at x=1/2; remaining analytic q terms decay exponentially. This contradicts the required central growth. The reader spells out the restricted coefficient convention.
